output.title: When a rollback drill earns its keep
output.body:
For a small business owner, the cost of a rollback drill is not abstract. It is the time and attention it takes to write down how to undo one workflow change before that change goes live.

That is a plain trade-off. You spend a little time now, or you discover the broken path later when the workflow is already carrying orders, customer data, or money-movement steps that still need human approval.

I would treat rollback drills as a bounded decision, not a ritual. If the workflow is simple and easy to rebuild, skip it. If one failure would force you into manual recovery or awkward re-entry work, a drill is probably worth the upfront time.

The practical next step is simple: pick one recurring workflow, define what rollback would mean in plain English, and test that rollback path once before you expand the build. That gives you a real answer instead of a guess.

Unglamorous, yes. Still cheaper than finding out the hard way.
